readings.title: Testing a reusable water filter
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
Students designed a simple reusable filter for muddy water. Early demonstrations looked successful, but groups used different amounts of water. The main obstacle was an experiment without consistent quantities. Colour changes were difficult to compare because sample sizes and waiting times varied. At first, the people involved did not agree on which part of the proposal deserved the most attention.

To investigate, the team used a controlled classroom procedure. Students measured equal samples and recorded the time and appearance after each stage. The organizers kept the first stage small enough to change without wasting substantial time or resources.

The evidence indicated the comparison became clearer but safety remained separate. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a display explaining limits of the model. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. The records were useful because they described ordinary use rather than an ideal situation imagined at a meeting.

The case suggests a broader point: a visible change does not prove water is safe to drink. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. The group published its reasons so that people who preferred a different result could still understand the choice. For those taking part in testing a reusable water filter, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: Why a bridge model bends
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A science club built paper bridges. One model held several books, while an apparently similar version bent under much less weight. The main obstacle was folding differences that were not recorded. The teams compared final shapes without noting how many layers or supports each bridge had. The question mattered to people with different schedules and levels of experience, so one account could not represent everyone.

To investigate, the team used measurements of material and loading position. Participants rebuilt models with the same paper and placed weights at marked points. A simple record of what happened each day gave the team a starting point for comparison.

The evidence indicated support placement strongly affected strength. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a construction log for each model. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. Some participants welcomed the change immediately, while others noticed practical details that needed further work.

The case suggests a broader point: fair experiments change one factor at a time. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. The result was a revised plan, not a claim that every difficulty had disappeared. For those taking part in why a bridge model bends, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: A sensor for classroom light
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A school tested a sensor that turned lights off when a classroom appeared empty. It sometimes darkened a room during quiet reading. The main obstacle was a sensor that missed still occupants. The device judged movement rather than actual use of the room. The initial idea sounded reasonable, yet the details of the place made it harder to carry out than expected.

To investigate, the team used observations during different lessons. Teachers recorded false shut-offs and asked pupils when the change interrupted work. Instead of relying on a single opinion, the team invited several users to describe what they actually did.

The evidence indicated quiet activities required a longer delay. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a revised setting and an easy manual override. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. This allowed the organizers to separate a temporary inconvenience from a pattern that required attention.

The case suggests a broader point: automation should account for human behaviour. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. They also decided when to check the arrangement again, because conditions could change over time. For those taking part in a sensor for classroom light, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: Making a bicycle bell clearer
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A design class explored bicycle bells for shared paths. A louder bell was noticed, but some pedestrians could not tell its direction. The main obstacle was sound volume confused with useful warning. The class had first measured loudness without asking walkers what they heard. The people affected were invited to comment before a permanent arrangement was chosen.

To investigate, the team used listening trials on a safe closed route. Participants stood at marked points and described which bell they could locate. The first trial produced both useful results and questions the team could not yet answer.

The evidence indicated a distinct tone improved recognition. The repeated observations mattered more than one unusual experience and changed how the team understood the situation. The group then introduced a bell design judged by clarity as well as volume. The revised approach was explained to users and given a date for a further practical check. Rather than hide those limits, the public note explained how the next version had been selected.

The case suggests a broader point: an invention succeeds only in real use. The experience connected a small local decision with a wider need to listen, measure and adjust. That explanation made later changes easier to discuss with residents and staff. For those taking part in making a bicycle bell clearer, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

translation.stem:
Translate the following passage into Chinese:
Projects concerning science and everyday inventions often begin with a practical question. People may agree on a general goal while experiencing the same service in different ways. In this case, local organizers invited residents to describe ordinary visits and kept simple records of what happened. They compared those accounts before changing the public science learning programme. The first trial did not answer every question, but it showed which difficulties were repeated and which were temporary. Staff then explained the reasons for a modest adjustment. Clear information helped people understand the decision, including those who would have preferred another option. The group planned to review the arrangement again after more people had used it.
translation.explanation: 参考译文供考生自评，注意语义准确、逻辑关系及汉语通顺。
translation.referenceAnswer: 有关科学发现与日常发明的项目通常从一个实际问题开始。人们可能赞同总体目标，却对同一服务有不同体验。在这个案例中，当地组织者请居民描述日常使用情况，并简单记录发生的事情。他们对照这些叙述后调整了服务。最初的试行无法回答所有问题，但能显示哪些困难反复出现，哪些只是暂时现象。工作人员随后解释了一项适度调整的原因。清楚的信息帮助人们理解决定，包括那些更希望采用其他方案的人。团队计划在更多人使用后再次评估安排。

writing.stem: Write at least 100 words in English to the science education team proposing a small improvement to the public science learning programme. Explain the problem, describe a short trial, and say what evidence should guide the final decision.
writing.explanation: 范文供考生自评，注意任务要点、组织结构及语言准确性。
writing.sampleAnswer:
Dear Committee Members,
I would like to propose a small improvement to the public science learning programme. People have noticed an experiment without consistent quantities, and a short trial could help us understand how often this problem occurs. We should ask regular users and people who have not used the service before to describe their experiences. Their comments may reveal details that a plan made in an office would miss.
For one month, staff could keep a simple record of participation, time spent and any difficulties reported. We should also explain the purpose of the trial in clear language so that residents know how to contribute. After the month, please publish a brief summary of both benefits and limits. The final decision should be based on what people actually experienced, with a date for checking the arrangement again.
Yours sincerely,
A resident
